noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: practical: investigate how enzyme activity can be affected by changes in temperature

primer.text: Amylase digesting starch into maltose is the classic enzyme practical, and iodine is the clock: every droplet transfer that still turns blue-black means starch remains. This note runs the temperature version — water baths from 30 to 60 degrees, repeats for reliability, the reading of results, the two named limitations with fixes, and the CORMS planning frame.

lessons.title: The amylase clock at different temperatures
lessons.opening: The method is a timing race: starch solution is warmed to the chosen temperature, amylase joins it, and every minute a droplet is transferred to a well of iodine. Blue-black means starch survives; the first well that stays yellow-brown marks the moment digestion finished. Repeating at each temperature and across a range builds the dataset.
keyPoints: Amylase digests starch into maltose, and iodine tests for remaining starch.
Iodine is yellow-brown and turns blue-black only while starch is present.
A droplet is transferred to a fresh iodine well every minute until no colour change occurs.
The reaction time is read by counting the wells up to the first unchanged one.
The whole run is repeated across a temperature range such as 30 to 60 degrees Celsius.

low.restatement: Mix amylase with warmed starch; test droplets against iodine every minute; count wells until iodine stops turning blue-black — that count is the digestion time at that temperature.
low.analogy: Iodine wells are bus stops: the reaction's bus travels along them once per minute, and the first stop where nothing changes is its final stop.
low.examPointer: When describing the method, name the interval (every minute) and the readout (counting wells) — both carry marks.

medium.restatement: The design fixes volume and concentration while varying temperature, and the iodine-well count converts a continuous reaction into a discrete, comparable number; repeats at each temperature expose the random error the stopwatch cannot see.
medium.analogy: Counting wells turns a blur into a ruler: each well is one tick of ten seconds' worth of clock on the tile.
medium.examPointer: State the controlled variables (volumes, concentrations) explicitly when asked why the comparison is fair.

check.stem: What does iodine turning blue-black in a well tell you during the practical?

options.text: Starch is still present in the droplet
The maltose is being built faster

check.stem: How is the reaction time recorded?

options.text: By the tube changing colour all at once
options.explanation: The tile, not the tube, is the readout.

options.text: By counting the wells up to the first one where iodine stays unchanged
options.explanation: Well counting is the stated readout.

options.text: By weighing the tube before and after

check.stem: What range of temperatures does the note suggest investigating?

options.explanation: Too cold for a visible rate spread.

check.stem: Why does the investigation repeat each temperature at least twice more?

options.text: To warm the water bath up
To use up the spare reagents
options.explanation: Reagent use is not a goal.

options.text: To check reliability by exposing random error in the timing

check.stem: Which variable set must stay controlled for the temperature comparison to be fair?

options.text: The volumes and concentrations of starch, amylase and iodine
options.explanation: The CORMS control list names these.
Temperature is the independent variable being changed.
The tile layout is fixed equipment, not a variable of interest.

check.stem: Name the enzyme and its substrate used in this practical.
State the colour iodine shows when starch has been fully digested.
Explain why the iodine wells must each receive a fresh droplet rather than re-testing the same well.
check.modelAnswer: Once a well's iodine has reacted with starch it cannot report a new state, so each timed droplet needs untouched iodine; re-using a well would mix old reaction products with the new droplet and blur the moment digestion truly finished.

check.stem: A pupil's 40-degree run shows the iodine still changing after 12 wells while the 37-degree run stopped at 5. Using enzyme theory, interpret the pattern.
check.modelAnswer: 40 degrees sits slightly above the human optimum, so the enzyme is already losing shape to early denaturation and digests the starch more slowly than at 37 — the longer well count at 40 matches the curve's fall beyond the peak.

lessons.title: Reading results, fixing limitations, planning with CORMS
lessons.opening: The analysis reads the well counts as reaction speeds: fewer wells means faster digestion, with the shortest count at the optimum temperature. Two limitations matter — drifting water temperature and judging colour by eye — and each has a named fix. CORMS then wraps the whole design into a planning answer examiners can mark quickly.
keyPoints: The shortest iodine-well count marks the optimum temperature, where the enzyme works fastest.
Below the optimum, colder temperatures slow collisions and stretch the reaction time.
A named limitation is temperature drift, fixed by using proper water baths at each set temperature.
A second limitation is judging colour by eye, improved by a colorimeter that measures colour intensity.
CORMS stands for Change, Organism, Repeat, Measure and control variables.

low.restatement: Fewest wells = fastest = optimum. Fix drifting temperature with water baths; fix colour judgement with a colorimeter. CORMS plans the design.
low.analogy: The well count is a race time: the temperature that wins with the fewest ticks is the enzyme's favourite.
low.examPointer: Pair each limitation with its improvement — a limitation stated without a fix earns half the marks.

medium.restatement: The two limitations attack validity and precision respectively: drift confounds which temperature caused the rate, and subjective colour calls blur the endpoint; baths and a colorimeter target each directly.
medium.analogy: Drift is an unfair referee (the wrong team blamed), colour-judgement is a fuzzy scoreboard (nobody knows who won); baths fix the referee, the colorimeter sharpens the scoreboard.
medium.examPointer: In CORMS answers, give M its letter explicitly (M1 time via wells; M2 the count itself) — the note models that format.

check.stem: Which temperature run should show the SHORTEST well count?

options.text: The run at the enzyme's optimum temperature

options.explanation: Heat denatures and slows or stops digestion.

check.stem: Which improvement fixes the drifting-temperature limitation?

options.text: Using water baths set to each temperature, with solutions pre-warmed
options.explanation: Water baths hold the temperature steady.

options.text: Adding more iodine to each well
options.explanation: Iodine volume does not fix drift.

check.stem: What does a colorimeter add to this investigation?

options.text: Extra amylase when the reaction slows
A record of the room's humidity
An objective measurement of colour intensity to detect the endpoint
options.explanation: The colorimeter replaces eye judgement with measurement.

options.text: A way to raise the temperature
options.explanation: That is the water bath's job.

check.stem: In the CORMS frame for this experiment, which letter covers repeating the investigation?
Which pairing of limitation and consequence is correct?

options.text: Temperature drift — the true temperature behind a rate is uncertain
options.explanation: Drift confuses the attribution of the measured rate.

options.text: Colour judgement — the enzyme digests faster
options.explanation: Judgement error adds noise, it does not speed digestion.
Baths prevent drift; they do not denature.

options.text: Colorimeter — it removes the need for amylase

check.stem: State what CORMS helps you do in a practical write-up.
check.modelAnswer: Plan a valid investigation: change, organism, repeat, measure, same/control variables.

check.stem: Name the instrument suggested for objective colour measurement.
Explain why the well-count method can miss the exact moment digestion finishes.
check.modelAnswer: Droplets are transferred only once per minute, so the endpoint is only known to fall somewhere inside a one-minute window between the last blue-black well and the first unchanged one; finer sampling intervals would narrow that window.

check.stem: A class runs the practical with baths at 30, 40 and 50 degrees and gets mean well counts of 9, 4 and 8. Which temperature sits nearest the optimum, and why does 50 still finish faster than 30?
check.modelAnswer: 40 degrees is nearest the optimum because its count of 4 is the shortest; 50 beats 30 because at 50 the enzyme still holds enough shape to work faster than the collision-starved 30-degree run, even though denaturation has begun eating into its rate.

The planning frame: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measure, Same/control variables.
